content: The accuracy of qualitative nucleic acid testing (NAT) methods compared to quantitative NAT methods for detecting and/or quantifying hepatitis C virus (HCV) RNA to confirm active HCV infection was evaluated through a systematic review. A literature search was conducted focusing on hepatitis C, diagnostic tests, and diagnostic accuracy. Studies were included if they assessed the sensitivity and specificity of a single qualitative HCV RNA test compared to a quantitative HCV RNA reference standard in humans. Two reviewers independently assessed the quality of the studies and extracted data to estimate test accuracy. Qualitative NAT assays for HCV RNA detection are at least 10 times more sensitive than quantitative assays. The lower limit of detection for most commercial qualitative assays is in the range of 10–15 IU/mL, as measured against a World Health Organization (WHO) standard. In contrast, the lower limit of detection for quantitative assays is between 600–1100 IU/mL. The sensitivity of quantitative HCV RNA assays ranges from 87% to 100% when compared to qualitative assays. Although qualitative assays have a lower limit of detection, the sensitivity range found in this review demonstrates that HCV viral loads are rarely in the lower range of detection limits for older quantitative assays. New technology platforms now offer linear quantification ranges between 12 and 108 IU/mL, eliminating the difference in detection limits between qualitative and quantitative assays. Additionally, new point-of-care (POC) devices for HCV viral load quantification are expected to become available soon. These devices are more affordable than laboratory-based assays and can potentially improve access to HCV detection and treatment monitoring. Rapid detection of HCV is critical to prevent the progression of the disease into its chronic phase. Both qualitative and quantitative NAT methods are essential for detecting active HCV infection, though there is limited research directly comparing the two methods for this purpose. Current guidelines provide recommendations on whom to screen for HCV and how to confirm infection but do not specify which tests are optimal for initial screening. The WHO has emphasized the global health importance of viral hepatitis through several resolutions. Advances in HCV detection technology create new opportunities for improving screening, referral, and treatment. This review focuses on individuals with detectable HCV antibodies to evaluate qualitative versus quantitative detection methods for confirming active HCV infection. The goal was to identify evidence on the sensitivity and specificity of qualitative HCV RNA tests compared to quantitative tests and to summarize key test characteristics associated with detecting active HCV infection. The systematic review included observational and randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that provided original data from patient specimens. Studies were eligible if they utilized commercially available HCV NAT tests and compared them to a quantitative HCV RNA reference standard. The reference standards included polymerase chain reaction (PCR), branched-chain DNA (bDNA), or transcription-mediated amplification (TMA). The performance characteristics of NATs were considered similar above 50 IU/mL, and all NATs were treated as a single reference standard. Sensitivity refers to the proportion of samples with true HCV infection diagnosed with positive qualitative NAT tests confirmed by positive quantitative NAT tests. Specificity refers to the proportion of samples with negative qualitative NAT tests confirmed by negative quantitative NAT tests. A database search was conducted across multiple platforms, including MEDLINE, EMBASE, PubMed, and others, with no language restrictions. Study selection involved three stages: screening titles/abstracts, assessing full manuscripts, and resolving differences between reviewers. Four studies met the inclusion criteria for the final analysis. Two studies were conducted in the United States, while the remaining two were in Taiwan and Germany. Only one study included a population at risk of HCV infection, while the others focused on patients with acute or chronic HCV infection. The review found that the lower limit of detection for most commercial qualitative assays was 10–15 IU/mL, while quantitative assays had a lower limit of 600–1100 IU/mL. Sensitivities of qualitative NAT methods ranged from 87% to 100%, with specificities between 97% and 100%. A significant limitation in the quality of the studies was the lack of information on the populations studied, randomization, sample collection, and standardization in evaluating diagnostic test accuracy. Qualitative NAT assays are highly sensitive for detecting the presence of the virus but do not provide information on viral load. They are essential for screening blood donors and monitoring treatment progression, as they indicate the presence of an ongoing HCV infection. Quantitative assays, on the other hand, are crucial for measuring viral load at the start of therapy and after 12 weeks of treatment to determine the effectiveness of further treatment. These assays have a broad dynamic range and can detect viral loads as low as 650 IU/mL, allowing for early response measurement during treatment. Recent advancements have improved the sensitivity of quantitative assays, with linear quantification ranges of 12–108 IU/mL and time-to-result ranging from 70 minutes to 5–6 hours. New POC platforms for HCV RNA quantification are being developed, offering cost-effective solutions that can be used outside laboratory settings. These devices are simple to operate, require minimal training, and have connectivity features for automated surveillance. Evaluating these POC platforms will be critical for determining their potential to improve access to HCV detection and treatment monitoring, particularly in resource-limited settings.
